title: [B1 • Band 5.0] Bài 313: Rewilding the Mind: Ecology and Control
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 313 (LEVEL B1 • BAND 5.0)

Rewilding the Mind: Ecology, Control, and Natural Process

Paragraph 1. Throughout most of the twentieth century, traditional nature conservation focused on tight human management. Parks were treated like museum displays that had to stay frozen in one historical period, usually the nineteenth century. Across Europe and North America, rangers hunted predators, removed fallen logs, and drained wetlands to maintain neat scenery for visitors. In his book Feral, environmental writer George Monbiot argues that this constant interference actually damaged ecosystems, creating weak landscapes that merely looked clean.

Paragraph 2. Monbiot promotes 'rewilding'—a philosophy that reduces human control so natural ecosystems can heal themselves. Rather than trying to copy a single past year, rewilding removes barriers and allows wildlife relationships to guide recovery. A central goal is returning top predators and key species such as wolves, lynx, and beavers. Without predators, plant-eating animals like deer multiply rapidly, eating young tree shoots and preventing forests from regenerating.

Paragraph 3. The most famous proof of rewilding occurred in Yellowstone National Park after gray wolves returned in 1995. Not only did wolves trim elk numbers, they completely changed how elk moved across the land. Fearing attacks, elk avoided open valleys and riverbanks, allowing willows and aspens to regrow within just a few years. Returning trees strengthened the soil, cooled river water for trout, and supplied timber for beavers, whose dams created ponds welcoming frogs and waterbirds. By changing elk behaviour, wolves literally reshaped Yellowstone's rivers.

Paragraph 4. Despite these successes, rewilding meets fierce resistance. Farming groups and sheep owners view rewilding as a serious danger to rural incomes and traditional countryside culture. Meanwhile, government environmental offices often feel uncomfortable with unpredictable wild spaces that ignore tidy management plans. Monbiot concludes that rewilding challenges our deep human desire to dominate nature, inviting us instead to live alongside independent wild systems.

q1.text: George Monbiot worked as a park ranger in North America before writing Feral.

steps: Đoạn 1: Chỉ nói Monbiot viết sách Feral phê bình cách quản lý cũ, không nói ông từng làm kiểm lâm.

q2.text: Twentieth-century park rangers protected wolves and kept wetlands wet for tourists.

steps: Đoạn 1: Kiểm lâm từng săn đuổi thú săn mồi và rút cạn đầm lầy (hunted predators... drained wetlands).

q3.text: Bringing back key species such as beavers and wolves is a core part of rewilding.

steps: Đoạn 2: "A central goal is returning top predators and key species such as wolves, lynx, and beavers."

q4.text: Government environmental offices welcome unpredictable wild landscapes.

steps: Đoạn 4: Các cơ quan này thường thấy không thoải mái (uncomfortable) với cảnh quan khó lường.

q5.text: Monbiot believes humans need to give up their urge to dominate the natural world.

steps: Đoạn 4: Thách thức khao khát thống trị tự nhiên để chung sống với hệ sinh thái tự vận hành.
